title: Baal of Peor and the Zeal of Phinehas
summary: While camped at Shittim, Israelite men begin sexual relations with Moabite women and join in the worship of Baal of Peor, and God's anger burns against Israel. As the people weep at the Tent of Meeting, an Israelite leader, Zimri, brazenly brings a Midianite woman, Cozbi, into his tent, and Phinehas the priest kills them both, stopping a plague that had killed 24,000. God grants Phinehas a covenant of peace and a lasting priesthood, and commands Israel to treat the Midianites as enemies.
story: The contrast with the previous three chapters is sharp and deliberate. On the heights above, Balaam has just declared that no curse or divination can touch Israel, that God sees no trouble in Jacob, and that the people are blessed. Down on the plain, Israel is doing what no curse could do: it is abandoning God on its own. Numbers 31:16 later reveals that this happened on Balaam's advice. The chapter is the last great rebellion of the wilderness period, and it falls on the new generation at the very edge of the promised land. It is followed by a second census (chapter 26), which confirms that the old generation has passed away and marks a fresh start. The zeal of Phinehas, the grandson of Aaron, also establishes the line of high priests that will continue into Israel's future.
historical:
Shittim, also called Abel-shittim (Numbers 33:49), was Israel's final camp on the plains of Moab before crossing the Jordan, and Joshua will send the spies from there (Joshua 2:1). Peor was a height nearby (compare 23:28), and Baal of Peor was the god worshiped there. Baal, meaning lord or master, was the title of the Canaanite storm and fertility god, and many local forms were worshiped under names tied to particular places. Moab's chief god was Chemosh (Numbers 21:29), so Baal of Peor may have been a local deity in Moabite territory, and scholars disagree on how the two were related.

The event cast a long shadow in Israel's memory. Deuteronomy 4:3-4 contrasts those who followed Baal of Peor and were destroyed with those who held fast to the LORD and were still alive. Hosea 9:10 names Baal-peor as the moment Israel first turned from God after a promising start, and Psalm 106:28-31 recalls both the sin and Phinehas's intervention. In the Maccabean revolt of the second century BC, the priest Mattathias was compared to Phinehas for his zeal (1 Maccabees 2:26), showing how the story shaped later Jewish ideas of zeal for the law.
cultural:
Religious feasts in the ancient world usually involved eating the meat of sacrifices in the presence of the god, so being invited to the sacrifices and eating (verse 2) meant sharing in the worship of that god. Some scholars think the sexual immorality was connected to fertility rites in Baal worship; others think the text describes intermarriage and ordinary sexual relations that drew the men into their partners' religion. Either way, the sin combined sexual unfaithfulness and idolatry, which the prophets would later treat as two sides of the same betrayal.

Zimri was not an ordinary Israelite but a leader of a Simeonite family (verse 14), and Cozbi was the daughter of a Midianite tribal chief (verse 15), so their union was a public act between leading families, carried out while the congregation wept at the sanctuary. The word used for the tent Phinehas entered (qubbah) occurs only here in the Bible; some scholars think it was a special tent or alcove, possibly a shrine, though the meaning is uncertain. Executing leaders in broad daylight (verse 4) was a public act of judgment, meant to turn away God's anger from the whole people.
literary: The chapter is built in two parts. Verses 1 to 9 tell the story: sin, God's anger, the command to execute the leaders, the brazen act, Phinehas's response, and the end of the plague. Verses 10 to 18 give God's interpretation: a covenant with Phinehas, the naming of the guilty pair, and the command against Midian. The words for zeal or jealousy (qanah and qin'ah) appear four times in verses 11 and 13, tying Phinehas's action to God's own jealousy for his people. The narrator withholds the names of Zimri and Cozbi until after the event, which gives their identities added weight. The number who died, 24,000, marks this as the deadliest judgment in the book.

outline.t: Israel joins in worshiping Baal of Peor
Phinehas acts and the plague is stopped
God's covenant of peace with Phinehas
The names of the slain and the command against Midian

doctrines.note: Israel's sin at Peor was the worship of another god, mixed with sexual unfaithfulness. The Bible repeatedly links the two, treating idolatry as spiritual adultery against the God who had bound himself to Israel in covenant.
God's jealousy for his people is not petty but the fierce love of a covenant partner. His holiness cannot tolerate his people's worship of other gods.
Verse 13 says Phinehas made atonement for the Israelites, turning away God's wrath. Atonement here involves the removal of guilt that has brought judgment on the whole community.

words.note: Tsamad, to join or yoke. Israel joined itself to Baal of Peor (verses 3 and 5). The verb pictures being yoked together, like animals in a harness, and suggests a binding attachment, the opposite of Israel's covenant loyalty to God.

Qin'ah, zeal or jealousy. God says Phinehas was zealous with God's own zeal (verse 11). The word describes intense, protective passion, whether good or bad; applied to God, it describes his exclusive love for his people.

Berit, covenant, a binding relationship with promises and obligations. God grants Phinehas “My covenant of peace”, a covenant of permanent priesthood for his descendants. Later texts trace the high priests through his line (1 Chronicles 6:4-15).
Shalom, peace, wholeness, well-being. The covenant of peace follows a violent act and ends a deadly plague. It restores right relationship between God and his people after the breach at Peor.

christ: The chapter's central pattern, God's wrath turned away from his people by someone who acts to make atonement, is taken up in the New Testament in a different form. Jesus shows zeal for God's house (John 2:17, quoting Psalm 69:9), but where Phinehas turned away wrath by executing the guilty, Christ turns it away by bearing it himself (Romans 3:25; 5:9). The covenant of peace given to Phinehas's line anticipates the prophets' promise of a covenant of peace (Ezekiel 34:25; 37:26), and Paul says that Christ himself is our peace, having reconciled people to God through the cross (Ephesians 2:14-16). The New Testament also recalls this chapter as a warning: Paul lists the immorality of Israel in the wilderness as an example for believers (1 Corinthians 10:8), and Revelation 2:14 names Balaam's teaching at Peor as a snare still threatening churches. These are thematic developments; Numbers 25 is not a prediction of Christ.

hard.q: Is Phinehas's killing of Zimri and Cozbi an endorsement of violent religious zeal?
hard.a:
The text praises Phinehas, which troubles many readers. Several points help place the story. Phinehas acts in the midst of a deadly plague, after God has commanded the judges to execute those who joined in Baal worship (verses 4 and 5), and against a leader who flaunted his sin before the weeping congregation. He is a priest, charged with guarding the sanctuary, and his act is presented as carrying out a judgment already decreed. Interpreters therefore generally read the story as a unique event in Israel's history, not a license for private violence in God's name.

The story was nonetheless used later to justify violent zeal, as in the Maccabean revolt and among some revolutionaries in the first century AD. The New Testament points in another direction. Paul had been a zealot who persecuted the church (Philippians 3:6), and after his conversion he redirected his zeal toward proclaiming Christ. Jesus rebuked disciples who wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village (Luke 9:54-55). There is also a discrepancy in numbers: Paul says 23,000 fell in one day (1 Corinthians 10:8), while verse 9 says 24,000 died in the plague; some explain the difference as including those executed by the judges or as counting different periods, and others see a slip in memory or a rounded figure.

questions: Israel was not defeated by Balaam's curse but by its own desires. Where are you more at risk from your own choices than from anything outside you?
God's jealousy is described as fierce love for his people. How does that change the way you hear the idea that God is jealous?
Phinehas's zeal was praised, but zeal has often been used to justify harm. How can we tell the difference between zeal for God and zeal for our own cause?
